metaDescription: Six woodworking dust collectors compared by airflow, filtration, bag size and mounting, with honest notes on rated versus real-world suction.
expertTake: The WEN DC1300 is the pick for a shop that runs a planer or a table saw with real chip volume, and the POWERTEC 800 CFM unit is the value choice for a one-tool-at-a-time garage. Anyone who only sands or runs a small bench saw should look at the wall-mounted units before spending on a large mobile machine. If you mostly use hand tools, a shop vacuum with a separator is the better answer and you can skip this category.
introParagraphs: A woodworking shop produces two very different wastes: coarse chips that fall straight down, and fine dust that stays airborne for hours. Chip collection is a volume problem and fine dust is a filtration problem, and most buyers shop for the first while suffering from the second.

Single-stage machines sit at the heart of home shops because they are affordable and move a lot of air for the money. They also rise or fall on three details that spec sheets bury: how much air survives once hose and bends are attached, how fine the filter is, and whether the bag can be emptied without making a fresh cloud.

products.name: WEN DC1300 1,300 CFM 14-Amp Dust Collector, 50-Gallon Bag
products.description:
This is the biggest machine in the lineup and the only one built around a tall vertical bag holding up to 50 gallons. The 14-amp motor drives a large impeller that the maker rates at 1,300 CFM, and the two 4 inch inlets let you plug a planer and a second tool into the same unit. That much bag volume matters more than it sounds, because chip-heavy machines like thickness planers fill a small bag in a single board.

The trade-off is that 1,300 CFM is measured with an open inlet, and a 4 inch hose with a couple of bends will cost you a large share of it. The 5 micron rating also means the finest dust passes through the bag and returns to the room, so this is a chip mover first and an air cleaner second. Against the WEN 7.4-amp unit, which claims 600 CFM, it moves roughly twice the air, but it also takes up a lot more floor.

Ownership is mostly about the bag. The tall bag is awkward to shake out, so expect to empty it outdoors or into a drum and wear a respirator while doing it. The mobile base makes it manageable to roll between a planer and a saw, but the footprint means a one-car garage has to give up a corner for it. Brushed motors on collectors at this price are loud, so ear protection is part of the package.
products.bestFor: A shop with a planer or jointer that fills bags fast and has room for a large mobile unit.
pros: Highest airflow rating in the lineup by a wide margin
50 gallon bag goes many boards between empties
Two 4 inch inlets serve a pair of tools
Mobile base lets it roll to the active machine
cons: 5 micron bag lets the finest dust recirculate
Large footprint and loud under load

products.name: POWERTEC 1 HP 800 CFM Dust Collector with 1 Micron Bag
products.description:
The POWERTEC puts an 800 CFM rating and a 1 micron upper bag onto a caster base roughly 15 by 25 inches. That combination is the reason it ranks high: the finer bag catches far more of the dust that actually harms lungs, while the airflow is still enough to pull chips from a table saw or a drill press.

It does not match the WEN DC1300 for volume, and it will struggle if you chain two machines through long hose runs. A 1 micron bag also loads faster than a 5 micron one, so suction falls off sooner and the bag needs more frequent attention. The maker also ships a second lower bag, which is the right layout, because the upper bag filters and the lower one collects.

Plan on shaking the upper bag clean every few sessions and checking the lower bag seal, since a loose clamp is where a lot of home-shop leaks start. Because the unit rolls on casters it is easy to park against a wall between jobs. It is the model to choose if one tool runs at a time and you care about air quality more than raw chip capacity.
products.bestFor: A garage woodworker who runs one machine at a time and wants finer filtration than a bargain bag.
pros: 1 micron bag filters far finer than most rivals
800 CFM rating is plenty for one tool
Caster base rolls easily between machines
Upper and lower bag layout is the right design
cons: Fine bag loads sooner and needs regular cleaning
Falls short with two tools or long hose runs

products.name: WEN 7.4-Amp Induction Motor Dust Collector, 15-Gallon Bag
products.description:
Its defining part is the induction motor. Induction motors run cooler and quieter than the brushed universal motors in cheaper collectors, and they have no brushes to wear out, so this is the machine you can leave running through a long sanding session without wanting to leave the room.

The 9 inch impeller gives it a 600 CFM rating, which sits below the POWERTEC 800 CFM unit on paper, but the larger impeller does not have to spin as fast for the same air. Bag capacity is 15 gallons, a middle size that suits sanders, a bandsaw and a small planer but not a heavy lumber dimensioning routine. You can run it on the mobile base or hang it on a wall, which is useful if floor space is short.

It is the better long-term machine than the brushed 5.7-amp model, mainly because the motor does not fade. Keep the filter bag clean, since a loaded bag makes even an induction motor draw more current. If you have a dedicated outlet you are better off, because motors in this class dislike long extension cords.
products.bestFor: A small shop where noise matters and the machine runs for long stretches.
pros: Induction motor runs cooler and quieter
Mobile base or wall mounting options
Large 9 inch impeller moves air without screaming
No brushes to wear out
cons: 600 CFM rating trails the larger machines
15 gallon bag fills fast on a planer

products.name: WEN DC3401 5.7-Amp Dust Collector, 12-Gallon Bag, Wall Mountable
products.description:
This is the smallest machine here, with an onboard handle and a 12-gallon bag. It uses a brushed motor to spin a 6 inch impeller and the maker rates it at 660 CFM, which is competitive with the larger 600 CFM induction model on paper because the smaller impeller spins faster.

The cost of that arrangement is noise and heat. Brushed motors scream compared to induction, and the brushes eventually need replacing. It is also the machine most likely to clog its bag on a planer, because 12 gallons is only a few boards. It suits a bench saw, a router table or a drill press, not a dimensioning workflow.

What it does better than anything else here is storage. The handle and the wall mount option mean it can disappear when not in use, which counts in a shared garage. Lift it by the handle, never by the hose, and empty the bag well before it is full, because a half-full bag already costs suction. Replace the brushes if you hear arcing or notice sparks inside the motor housing.
products.bestFor: A tight garage with a small saw and router table that needs a collector you can put away.
pros: Smallest footprint with a carrying handle
Wall mount option frees the floor
Single 4 inch port suits one tool
Good first collector for light use
cons: Brushed motor is loud and wears
12 gallon bag fills quickly on chip-heavy tools

products.name: VEVOR 1 HP 560 CFM Wall-Mount Dust Collector, 21-Gallon Bag
products.description:
The VEVOR is built to hang on a stud wall, which keeps the whole machine off the floor. It pairs a 1 HP motor and a 560 CFM rating with a 21-gallon non-woven bag and a 2.5 micron filter, so the filtration is finer than the 5 micron WEN bag and the bag is larger than the other compact units.

Its compromise is mobility. Once mounted it stays on one wall, which means you either run a hose to each machine or move the machine to the dust. It works well in a small shop where the major machines cluster near one wall. Its 560 CFM rating is lower than the POWERTEC 800 CFM unit, so a long hose run will starve it.

Mounting is the main ownership task. Hang it on studs rather than drywall anchors, because a full 21 gallon bag is heavy and the vibration loosens weak fasteners. Empty the bag at the halfway mark and inspect the non-woven bag for pinholes, since torn cloth quietly defeats the 2.5 micron rating.
products.bestFor: A fixed-layout shop with machines clustered along one wall.
pros: 2.5 micron filter beats a typical 5 micron bag
21 gallon bag is generous for the size
Wall mounting recovers floor space
1 HP motor handles a small machine cluster
cons: Fixed to one wall, so hose runs get long
560 CFM rating is modest for a planer

products.name: DYNAVEX 10-Amp Dust Extractor, 12-Gallon Tank, HEPA Filter
products.description:
This one is a different animal: a hose-and-tank extractor with a HEPA filter and a switch that starts the machine when the connected tool starts. It is meant for sanders, track saws and routers where fine dust is the problem and chip volume is low, and a HEPA filter is the correct answer to that problem.

It cannot do what the bag collectors do. A 12 gallon tank and a vacuum-style motor will not keep up with a thickness planer, and the narrow hose limits how much air it moves compared with the 800 CFM units. Think of it as a precision tool for fine dust rather than a chip mover, closer in function to a shop vacuum with automatic switching.

The linked switch is the feature that saves effort, because the extractor spins up and down with the sander so you never forget it. Empty the tank before it fills so the HEPA filter does not clog, and wash or replace the filter per the maker's schedule. It pairs well with a bag collector, which handles the heavy machines while this deals with sanding.
products.bestFor: Sanding, routing and track saw work where fine dust matters more than chip volume.
pros: HEPA filter captures the finest dust
Linked switch starts with the tool
Wheels make it easy to move around
Low-volume work stays cleaner than with a bag
cons: Tank is too small for planer or jointer chips
Airflow cannot match the bag collectors

buyingCriteria.explanation: A dust collector's CFM rating is measured with the inlet wide open, and the number falls the moment you attach hose, bends and a blast gate. A 4 inch flexible hose is far more restrictive than smooth duct, so the WEN DC1300 at 1,300 CFM may deliver well under that at the tool. Treat the rating as a ceiling and compare machines by impeller size and motor power too. As a rough rule, a machine rated near 800 CFM like the POWERTEC suits one machine, and anything chaining two tools wants the larger WEN DC1300.

Fine dust under 10 microns is what lodges in lungs, and a bag that only stops 5 micron particles passes the worst of it straight back to the room. The WEN DC1300 uses a 5 micron bag, the VEVOR claims 2.5 micron, and the POWERTEC ships a 1 micron bag. Finer bags clog sooner, so the benefit comes with more shaking and cleaning. Buyers who sand a lot should favour the finer bag or the DYNAVEX HEPA extractor over a larger machine with a coarse one.

A thickness planer can fill a small bag in a single board, and a full bag cuts suction dramatically. The WEN DC1300 holds 50 gallons, the VEVOR 21, the WEN 7.4-amp 15 and the WEN DC3401 only 12. Pick bag size around your heaviest chip maker, not your lightest. Emptying is the other half: a clean-looking bag that is awkward to empty creates a dust cloud, so wear a respirator and empty outdoors.

Induction motors run quieter and longer than the brushed universal motors that cheaper machines use. The WEN 7.4-amp induction unit is the quietest here, while the 5.7-amp brushed DC3401 spins faster and is louder. Brushed motors also need new brushes eventually. If you run a collector for long sanding sessions, noise is a daily cost rather than a one-time inconvenience, so it is worth paying for an induction motor.

A collector on casters can follow the active machine, which shortens hose runs and keeps airflow high. A wall-mounted unit like the VEVOR saves floor but forces long hoses or a fixed machine layout. Short hose is the cheapest way to gain real CFM, so mobility is worth more than it looks. If you mount a unit, find studs, because a full bag is heavy.

Most of these machines use a 4 inch port, which suits a table saw or router table but starves a planer that really wants 6 inches or a larger bore. The WEN DC1300 offers two 4 inch inlets, which helps with two small tools but is not equivalent to a 6 inch main. Use the shortest, smoothest hose you can, and avoid sharp elbows; each one costs air. Reducers also cost airflow, so match hose to the tool port.

specDecoder.meaning: Cubic feet of air moved per minute with the inlet open. It falls as resistance rises from hose and bends.
specDecoder.watchFor: The WEN DC1300 at 1,300 CFM and the VEVOR at 560 CFM are not comparable once both sit behind identical hose.

specDecoder.meaning: The smallest particle size the filter is rated to catch. Lower numbers mean finer filtration and faster loading.
specDecoder.watchFor: The POWERTEC 1 micron bag is much finer than the WEN DC1300 5 micron bag.

specDecoder.meaning: Motor load figures that hint at power but do not guarantee airflow. Impeller design decides how much work becomes airflow.
specDecoder.watchFor: The 14-amp WEN DC1300 and 7.4-amp WEN induction unit differ by far more than the amps suggest.

specDecoder.meaning: How much dust the bag holds before suction falls. Bigger bags mean fewer interruptions.
specDecoder.watchFor: The DC3401 holds 12 gallons against the DC1300 at 50, so planer work suits one and not the other.

specDecoder.meaning: The fan wheel inside the housing. Larger wheels move more air at lower speed and noise.
specDecoder.watchFor: The WEN 9 inch impeller is the largest among the small units and explains its quiet running.

howWeEvaluated.title: Airflow versus restriction
howWeEvaluated.description: We read each spec sheet for rated CFM, impeller size and port count. Then we judged how that airflow would survive a realistic hose run. The WEN DC1300 at 1,300 CFM led the field, with the POWERTEC at 800 CFM leading the 1 HP class.

howWeEvaluated.title: Filtration quality
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared stated micron ratings and bag construction, because filtration decides how much fine dust returns to the room. Finer bags earned credit while their faster loading was counted against them. The 1 micron POWERTEC bag and the HEPA DYNAVEX filter ranked highest here.

howWeEvaluated.title: Capacity and emptying
howWeEvaluated.description: We weighed bag or tank size against the chip volume of typical machines. Bigger bags mean fewer interruptions, but awkward emptying costs points. The 50 gallon WEN and 21 gallon VEVOR scored best.

howWeEvaluated.title: Noise and motor design
howWeEvaluated.description: We looked at induction versus brushed motors and the likely sound under load. Quieter, longer-lived motors earned higher ratings for daily use. The WEN induction unit stands out against the brushed DC3401.

howWeEvaluated.title: Footprint and mounting
howWeEvaluated.description: Garage shops live and die by floor space. We assessed casters, handles and wall mounting, and the real hose reach each allows. Mobility counted because short hose preserves airflow.

cards.label: Bag collector
cards.text: A bag collector like the WEN DC1300 or POWERTEC moves a large volume of air and holds a lot of chips. Its weakness is fine dust, which depends entirely on bag micron rating. Choose this for sawing, planing and jointing.

cards.label: HEPA extractor
cards.text: The DYNAVEX captures the finest dust and starts with the tool, but its tank and hose are small. It suits sanders and routers where dust is fine and chips are few.

howToChoose.note: Planer owners pick the bag collector; sanding-heavy shops pick the extractor; many shops run both.

rows: Supports mobile base or wall mount

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: Planers throw huge chip volumes, so look for the largest bag and the most airflow, ideally with a short, wide hose to the planer port. Avoid collectors with small bags that need emptying every few boards.

cards.label: In this comparison
cards.text: The WEN DC1300 is the clear answer, with 50 gallons of bag and the highest airflow rating. The POWERTEC 800 CFM is the cheaper fallback if you plane occasionally and empty often.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: Spend more if you plane lumber regularly or run two machines at once, because the WEN DC1300 buys real capacity. Also spend more if you sand heavily and want an induction motor or a HEPA extractor in place of a cheap bag.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: Save if you run a small saw and a router table a few hours a week; the WEN DC3401 or VEVOR will do the job. Pair it with a respirator and you cover most of the safety gap.

maintenance.why: Suction drops sharply as the bag fills. Empty outdoors and wear a respirator.

maintenance.task: Shake or clean the filter bag
maintenance.why: Fine dust packs the cloth and cuts airflow. A 1 micron bag needs this far more often than a 5 micron one.
A loose clamp between bags leaks dust into the room. Check the lower bag ring and any tape joints.
The DC3401 uses a brushed motor and brushes wear out. Replace them when you see arcing.
A full bag is heavy and vibration loosens fasteners. Make sure wall mounts sit on studs.

faq.q: Is a single-stage collector enough for a home shop?
faq.a: For most hobby shops, yes. A single-stage machine like the POWERTEC or WEN handles chips well, and a fine bag improves air quality. A cyclone separator ahead of it keeps the bag cleaner for longer.

faq.q: How much airflow do I really need?
faq.a: A single tool on a 4 inch hose is well served by a machine rated near 800 CFM. Planers and anything on longer duct want more. Rated figures fall with hose length, so shop with margin.

If you sand or cut sheet goods, yes, because fine dust is the health risk. The tradeoff is faster loading, so you will clean the bag more often. A coarse 5 micron bag mostly protects the motor rather than your lungs.

faq.q: Can I use a shop vacuum instead?
faq.a: For small tools, a vacuum with a good filter works well. A vacuum cannot move the chip volume a planer produces. A dust collector handles volume, while a vacuum or HEPA extractor handles fine dust.

faq.q: How long do these machines last?
faq.a: Induction motors can run for many years with little attention. Brushed motors need new brushes sooner and run louder. Bags and clamps are the usual wear items.

faq.q: Is wood dust a fire risk?
faq.a: Fine dust can ignite in unusual conditions, so keep collectors away from grinders and welding sparks. Empty bags regularly and do not let dust pile up around the motor.
